unit.title: Use and maintain graduated measuring devices

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: A drawing gives a shaft size as 40.00 ± 0.05 mm, so the tolerance band is 0.10 mm. Which device is the best choice to check it?
options: A steel rule read carefully to the nearest 0.5 mm
A 25–50 mm micrometer reading to 0.01 mm
A vernier caliper reading to 0.05 mm
A steel tape measure with a 1 mm scale

questions.stem: Many workshops use a "rule of ten" when choosing a measuring device for a job. What does this rule say?
options: Check each device against a standard every ten days
Take ten readings of each size and record the highest
Keep every device at least ten metres from welding bays
Resolution should be a tenth of the tolerance band

questions.stem: A metric vernier caliper reads to 0.05 mm. The main scale shows 32 mm before the vernier zero, and the 9th vernier line lines up with a main scale line. What is the reading?
On a dial caliper, one full turn of the needle is 1 mm. The beam shows 18 mm and the needle points to 36 on the dial (0.01 mm divisions). What is the reading?

questions.topic: Care of devices in a welding shop
questions.stem: Why must a digital caliper never touch a part that is being arc welded, or that is still connected to the welding return lead?
options: The display would change to inches without warning
The beam could bend under the weight of the lead
Welding current could pass through and ruin it
The battery would charge too fast and swell

questions.stem: A metric micrometer has a vernier on its sleeve and reads to 0.001 mm. The sleeve shows 8.5 mm, the thimble reads 23, and the 4th vernier line lines up. What is the reading?
How is the zero of a 25–50 mm outside micrometer checked before use?
options: Close the faces together and look for 0.00
Measure the anvil of a 0–25 mm micrometer
Compare it with a steel rule at the 25 mm mark
Measure the 25 mm setting standard made for it

questions.stem: Why must extra care be taken when reading a depth micrometer?
options: It can only be read with the part still warm
Its sleeve scale reads the opposite way
It has no thimble, so it is read on a dial
It reads only in whole millimetres

questions.stem: A bush must have a bore of 80.00 mm, checked to 0.01 mm. Which device is best for the job?
options: An inside micrometer or a dial bore gauge
A steel rule held across the end face
The hook end of a steel tape measure
An outside micrometer of the right size range

questions.stem: A dial indicator has 100 divisions round its face, and one full turn of the needle is 1 mm. What is each division worth?
options: 0.1 mm
1 mm

questions.stem: A shaft is turned slowly with a dial indicator resting on it. The needle swings between −0.04 mm and +0.06 mm. What is the total indicator reading (the run-out)?
How should the plunger of a plunger-type dial indicator be set against the surface being checked?
options: At about 45° so that it slides easily
Just touching, with no pre-load at all
Square to the surface, with a little pre-load
Lying flat along the surface, parallel to the work

questions.stem: A vernier height gauge is used on a surface plate to check the height of holes in a bracket. What does the surface plate give?
options: A magnetic hold so the part cannot slide about
A warm base that keeps parts at 20 °C
A printed scale to read heights from
A flat reference surface to measure from

questions.stem: Precise measurements, gauge blocks and setting standards are all referred to one standard temperature. What is it?
Steel grows about 0.012 mm per metre for each 1 °C rise in temperature. A 2 m steel bar is measured in the yard at 35 °C. How much longer is it than it would be at 20 °C?
When an outside size is measured with a vernier caliper, where should the work sit in the jaws for the most accurate reading?
options: Right at the tips of the jaws, where they are thinnest
As close to the beam as the jaws allow
Between the small inside (knife) jaws
Wherever it is easiest to hold steady

questions.stem: Which graduated device is used to check the leg length and throat size of a finished fillet weld?
options: A feeler gauge
A fillet weld gauge
A radius gauge
A depth micrometer

questions.stem: A bridge cam (multi-purpose) weld gauge is used on a finished butt weld. Which of these can it measure?
options: The hardness of the weld metal
The current that was used
The strength of the joint
The cap height above the plate

questions.stem: A weld gauge shows undercut 0.8 mm deep. The welding procedure allows no more than 0.5 mm. What should the inspector do?
options: Accept it, because it is still under 1 mm deep
Grind the weld cap flush and pass it
Record it as out of limit and report it
Measure it again with a tape measure

questions.stem: On a pipe joint that has been fitted up for welding, what does a hi-lo gauge measure?
options: How far the inside surfaces are out of line
The bevel angle cut on the end of one pipe only
The wall thickness after welding
The outside diameter of each pipe

questions.stem: A welding procedure calls for a 2.5 mm root gap. The team has a set of feeler gauges. How is the gap best checked?
options: Stack blades that add up to 2.5 mm and slide them in
Measure across the outside of both plates with a caliper
Use a tape measure held across the joint
Push one 0.25 mm blade in ten times

questions.stem: A universal bevel protractor reads to 5 minutes (5′). The main scale shows 37° and the vernier line for 25′ lines up. What is the angle?
A 5 m tape is checked against the Centre's reference tape and reads 2 mm long over its length. What should be done?
options: Bend the end hook back by 2 mm
Use it only on lengths over 3 m from now on
File 2 mm off the end of the hook
Take it out of use, tag it and report it

questions.stem: What should a calibration certificate for a micrometer show?
options: The price paid and the name of the shop
The errors found at each test point, and the date
The name of the trainee who uses it most
The colour of the case it should always be kept in

questions.stem: At its calibration check, a micrometer is found to read 0.05 mm too large. Besides taking it out of use, what must the supervisor do?
options: Nothing more, because the error is small
Reset its zero and put it back in use with no record kept
Scrap every part the team has ever made
Review parts measured with it since its last good check

questions.stem: A vernier caliper has an in-date calibration label, but it was dropped on the shop floor this morning. What should happen?
options: Use it, because the label is still in date
Have it checked before it is used again
Use it only for rough work for today
Wait for the next due date to check it

questions.stem: What is meant by "wringing" gauge blocks?
options: Sliding clean blocks together so they cling as one stack
Twisting the blocks hard to test that they are properly hardened
Wiping off the old oil with a dry rag before storing
Clamping the blocks in a vice so they cannot move

questions.stem: Why should gauge blocks be handled as little as possible, and with a clean cloth or gloves?
options: So that they do not get lost
Because their edges are very sharp and can cut the skin
Hand heat and sweat change their size and cause rust
Because they are strongly magnetic

questions.stem: Measuring devices are kept in the welding and fabrication shop. Which way of storing them is best?
options: On the welding bench, ready for quick use at all times
In the main toolbox, packed in with hammers and files
In their cases, in a closed cabinet away from spatter and dust
On a sunny window sill, where the damp air can never reach them

questions.topic: Care of devices in a welding shop
questions.stem: A vernier caliper keeps picking up fine steel filings on its jaws. What is the most likely cause?
options: It has become magnetised
Its battery is running low
It is out of calibration
Its locking screw is loose

questions.stem: Which entry on an inspection sheet gives the most useful record of a measurement?
options: 24.36 mm, caliper VC-03, by K. Brown
Within tolerance, checked by eye
About 24 mm, see me

questions.stem: A digital caliper shows readings in 0.01 mm steps, but the maker states its accuracy as ±0.03 mm. What does this mean?
options: Every reading is right to 0.01 mm
It moves in 0.03 mm steps only
It can measure up to 0.03 m only
A reading may be up to 0.03 mm out

questions.stem: An inspector measures a machined pin with a micrometer at both ends and in two directions at each end. Why?
options: To use up the inspection time
To find any taper or out-of-round
To warm up the micrometer first
To wear in the new micrometer faces evenly

questions.stem: A 9 m long beam is measured with a steel tape. Which method gives the most accurate result?
options: Let the tape hang in a curve between the two ends of the beam
Hook the tape over a rough, uncut end of the beam
Lay the tape flat along the beam and pull it straight
Measure in 1 m steps with a steel rule and add them

questions.stem: A new team member reads a vernier caliper with the work at the jaw tips and the caliper tilted. What should you, as the team leader, do first?
options: Show the right method and have them measure again
Take over and do all of the measuring yourself
Report them to the manager for poor work
Let them carry on so they learn from mistakes

questions.stem: A procedure says the plate must be at least 100 °C before welding. Which device gives an actual reading, in degrees, of the plate temperature?
options: A temperature-indicating crayon
A glass thermometer held in the air nearby
The colour of the steel near the joint
A contact (surface) thermometer

questions.stem: A drawing gives every hole position from edge A, marked as the datum. An inspector measures them from edge B instead. What is the risk?
options: Any error in the overall length is added to each hole
The holes will be measured far too accurately to be useful
None, because both edges were cut straight
The caliper will start reading in inches

questions.stem: An engineer's square is held on a welded corner, and a thin gap of light shows at the top of the blade. Which device measures the size of that gap?
options: A steel tape measure
A vernier height gauge
A bevel protractor
A set of feeler gauges

questions.stem: A round bar measures about 62 mm across. Which outside micrometer should be used?
Why are digital calipers often chosen for checking a large batch of parts in a busy shop?
options: They never need calibration
They are quick to read and can be zeroed anywhere
They do not need a battery
Dirt and grit on the jaws do not affect their readings

questions.stem: A digital caliper is zeroed on a 50.00 mm setting piece, then closed on a part. The display shows −0.12. What is the size of the part?
What should be used to clean the measuring faces of a micrometer just before use?
options: A clean, lint-free cloth
A strip of fine emery cloth
A soft brass wire brush
A blast from the air line

questions.stem: Why is a micrometer stored with its faces a little apart, not screwed closed?
options: So that it is easier to pick up
To keep the ratchet spring wound up
So heat changes cannot strain the frame and faces
To show the stores team that it has been used that day

questions.stem: Your team's inspection finds that 3 of 20 brackets are over the length tolerance. What is the right next step?
options: Pass the whole batch, since 17 of the 20 are good
Label and set the 3 aside, then record and report them
Grind the 3 to size quietly and send the whole batch out
Measure the 3 again with a tape until they pass

questions.stem: A 75–100 mm micrometer reads 75.012 mm on its 75.000 mm setting standard. Until it is adjusted, what correction applies to readings near 75 mm?
options: Add 0.012 mm
Add 0.12 mm
Subtract 0.12 mm
Subtract 0.012 mm

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences and show any working. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is the name of the very flat, heavy plate of granite or cast iron used as the datum when checking heights with a height gauge?
A vernier caliper reads to 0.05 mm. The main scale shows 41 mm and the 7th vernier line lines up. What is the reading, in mm?
In dial indicator work, what do the letters TIR stand for?
The first 10 mm of a steel rule is worn, so a trainee measures from the 10 mm mark. The far end of the part is at 157 mm on the rule. What is the true length, in mm?
What is the name of the set of thin blades, each cut to an exact curve, used to check the radius of a corner or the shape of a weld toe?
A metric micrometer reads to 0.01 mm. The sleeve shows 13.5 mm and the thimble reads 42. What is the reading, in mm?
What one word describes the unbroken chain of comparisons that links a workshop device back to a national measurement standard?
What is the name of the fixed part of a micrometer, under the thimble, that carries the scale marked in 0.5 mm steps?
A dial indicator reads 0.01 mm per division, and one turn is 1 mm. The needle moves 2 full turns and then 35 more divisions. How far has the plunger moved, in mm?
What is the name of the report raised when a part is found not to meet the drawing or specification? (Give its full name or its letters.)
How many minutes of angle are there in a quarter of a degree (0.25°)?
What is the name for the largest and smallest sizes a part may be, such as 49.95 mm and 50.05 mm?
What is the name of the unit of length that is one thousandth of a millimetre?
What type of caliper shows its reading as numbers on a small electronic screen?
A size is given on a drawing as 120 +0.0 / −0.4 mm. What is the smallest acceptable size, in mm?

essays.stem: Your team must inspect a welded bracket. The drawing gives the overall length as 600 ± 2 mm, a bored hole as 25.00 ± 0.05 mm, a bevel angle of 30° ± 2°, and 6 mm fillet welds. Plan the inspection: say which device you would use for each feature, and explain why.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first read the drawing and list each feature with its size and tolerance, then choose a device that reads about ten times finer than the tolerance band, as long as it suits the job. The overall length has a band of 4 mm, so a steel tape or a long steel rule that reads to 1 mm or 0.5 mm is good enough, used from the datum edge with the tape laid flat. The bored hole has a band of 0.10 mm, so I would use an inside micrometer or a bore gauge reading to 0.01 mm; a vernier caliper is too coarse. The 30° bevel has a band of 4°, so a bevel protractor or the angle scale on a weld gauge will do. The 6 mm fillets are checked with a fillet weld gauge for leg length and throat. I would check that every device is clean, zeroed and in date, measure at room temperature after the part has cooled, and record each result with the device number.
markingPoints: Lists each feature and its tolerance from the drawing before choosing
Uses the idea that the device should read about ten times finer than the tolerance band
Correct choices: tape or rule for length, inside micrometer or bore gauge for the hole, protractor for the bevel, fillet gauge for welds
Explains why a coarser device (for example a vernier caliper for the hole) is not good enough
Checks devices are clean, zeroed and in date; measures cool parts; records with the device number

essays.stem: Describe how you would carry out an in-house check of a 0–150 mm vernier or digital caliper using gauge blocks, and how you would record the result.
essays.modelAnswer: I would do the check in a clean, cool place, with the caliper and the gauge blocks left together for a while so they are at the same temperature. First I clean the jaws and look for damage, burrs or a bent jaw, check that the slide moves smoothly, and close the jaws to check that the zero reads 0.00 with no light showing between them. Then I measure gauge blocks, or stacks of blocks, at several points across the range, for example 10, 50, 100 and 150 mm, holding each block deep in the jaws with light, even pressure. I check the inside jaws on a ring gauge or a set size and the depth rod on a block on the surface plate. For each point I write down the true size, the reading and the error, and compare the errors with the Centre's limit. If all are inside the limit, I sign and date the record and fit a new label with the next due date. If not, I tag it out of use and report it.
markingPoints: Prepares: clean place, devices at the same temperature, visual and zero checks
Measures gauge blocks at several points across the full range
Checks inside jaws and depth rod as well as the outside jaws
Records true size, reading and error for each point, and compares with the allowed limit
Labels with date and next due date if it passes; tags out and reports if it fails

essays.stem: Explain how to set up and use a dial indicator to check a machined flange face for run-out (wobble) while it turns, and how you would report the result.
essays.modelAnswer: I would mount the flange so it can turn true on its centre, for example on a shaft in a lathe chuck or between centres, and make sure the face is clean and free of burrs and spatter. I fix the dial indicator to a magnetic base or stand on a rigid part of the machine, with the plunger square to the flange face, near the outer edge, and with a small pre-load so the needle has moved about a quarter of a turn. I turn the bezel to set the needle to zero. Then I turn the flange slowly by hand through one full turn and watch the needle, noting the highest and lowest readings. The total indicator reading is the difference between them; for example, from −0.03 to +0.05 mm is 0.08 mm. I repeat the check to be sure. I record the result, the position checked and the device number, compare it with the drawing limit, and report whether the flange is accepted or needs correcting.
markingPoints: Mounts the part to turn true and cleans the face
Fixes the indicator rigidly, plunger square to the surface, with a little pre-load
Zeros the bezel and turns the part slowly through a full turn
Works out the TIR as the difference between highest and lowest readings, with an example
Repeats, records with the device number, compares with the limit and reports

essays.stem: A 6 m steel beam is measured in the yard on a hot afternoon, when the steel is at 40 °C. Steel grows about 0.012 mm per metre for each 1 °C. Work out how much longer the beam is than at 20 °C, and explain the other ways heat can upset measurements in a welding shop and how to control them.
essays.modelAnswer: The steel is 40 − 20 = 20 °C above the standard temperature. The growth is 6 m × 20 °C × 0.012 mm = 1.44 mm, so the beam measures about 1.4 mm longer than it would at 20 °C. On a tight tolerance this could make a good beam look wrong, or hide a real error. Heat causes other problems too. A part that has just been welded or flame-cut is hot and has grown, and it may move again as it cools and distorts, so final measurements are taken only when it is back to room temperature. A steel tape left in the sun also grows, but not always by the same amount as the work. Holding a micrometer or gauge block in a warm hand for a long time makes it grow. To control this, I measure in the shade or early in the day where possible, let parts and devices settle to the same temperature, hold devices by their insulated parts, and note the temperature on the record when the tolerance is tight.
markingPoints: Correct calculation: 6 × 20 × 0.012 = 1.44 mm (about 1.4 mm)
Explains the effect on accepting or rejecting the beam
Hot parts after welding or cutting grow and distort: measure when cool
Devices also change with heat (tape in sun, hand heat on micrometers and gauge blocks)
Controls: shade, same temperature for part and device, insulated handling, record temperature

essays.stem: Describe how you would use weld gauges to inspect a batch of fillet and butt welds, and how you would record the results against the acceptance limits.
essays.modelAnswer: Before I start, I get the drawing and the welding procedure, so I know the sizes and the acceptance limits for each weld, and I check that the gauges are clean, undamaged and in date. The welds must be cool and the slag and spatter removed. For fillet welds, I use a fillet weld gauge to check that each leg is at least the size on the drawing and that the throat is right, and I look at whether the face is too convex or concave. For butt welds, I use a bridge cam gauge to measure the cap height above the plate, the depth of any undercut, and any misalignment between the plates. On pipe, I can use a hi-lo gauge at fit-up to check that the inside surfaces line up. I measure at several places along each weld, especially at starts and stops. I record each weld's number, the readings and whether it is accepted, and I mark any weld that is out of limit, tag the part and write a non-conformance report.
markingPoints: Gets the drawing, procedure and limits; checks gauges; welds clean and cool
Fillet gauge used for leg length and throat (and face shape)
Bridge cam gauge used for cap height, undercut and misalignment (hi-lo gauge for pipe fit-up)
Measures at several points, including starts and stops
Records weld number, readings and result; marks and reports welds that are out of limit

essays.stem: Explain how you would set up a calibration system for the measuring devices used by the Centre's welding team.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would list every graduated device in a register: tapes, rules, calipers, micrometers, dial indicators, protractors, weld gauges and thermometers. Each device gets its own number, marked on it or its case, so it can be traced. For each one, the register shows its range, resolution, where it is kept and how often it must be checked. The interval depends on how much it is used, how accurate it must be and its past results; a busy caliper might be checked every three months and a little-used gauge yearly. Some checks can be done in-house against gauge blocks and setting standards that are themselves calibrated by an accredited laboratory, so the chain is traceable. Each device gets a label with its number and next due date, and the results go into the register. A device that fails, or is damaged or overdue, is tagged out of use and kept apart. The supervisor then checks the parts measured with it since its last good check.
markingPoints: A register of all devices, each with its own identification number
Intervals set by use, accuracy needed and past results
Traceable checks: in-house against calibrated standards, or an accredited laboratory
Labels with due dates and results recorded
Failed, damaged or overdue devices tagged out, and earlier work reviewed

essays.stem: Compare vernier, dial and digital calipers. For each, give one advantage and one drawback, and say which you would choose for a busy batch inspection and why.
essays.modelAnswer: A vernier caliper has no battery or gears, so it is tough and works in heat, dust and damp, and it keeps its accuracy well. Its drawback is that it is slow to read, and it is easy to misread the vernier lines, especially in poor light or for someone with weak eyesight. A dial caliper is quicker to read, because the fine part of the reading is shown by a needle on a dial. Its drawback is that the rack and gears can be damaged by dirt, grit or a knock, and the needle can jump a tooth and give a false zero. A digital caliper is the quickest and easiest to read, can switch between millimetres and inches, and can be zeroed at any point to compare parts with a master. Its drawbacks are that it needs a battery, and it can be damaged by water, magnetism or welding current. For a busy batch inspection I would choose a digital caliper, because it is fast and reduces reading mistakes, but I would check its zero often and keep a vernier as a back-up.
markingPoints: Vernier: tough and needs no battery, but slow and easy to misread
Dial: quicker to read, but gears can be damaged by dirt or knocks
Digital: fastest, can zero anywhere and switch units, but needs a battery and is easily damaged
Sensible choice for batch work with a reason
Mentions checking the zero often or keeping a back-up

essays.stem: You are training a new team member to use a 0–25 mm outside micrometer. Describe how you would teach the skill and how you would check that they are competent.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by explaining what the micrometer is for, its range and how fine it reads, and naming the parts: frame, anvil, spindle, sleeve, thimble, ratchet and lock. I would show how to clean the faces and check the zero. Then I would demonstrate a measurement step by step: hold the frame by its insulated part, place the work square between the anvil and spindle, close it with the ratchet until it clicks two or three times, lock it if needed, and read the sleeve and then the thimble. I would explain the reading out loud, for example 7.5 plus 0.38 equals 7.88 mm. Next the trainee does it while I watch, and I correct any faults, such as forcing the thimble or reading from the side. To check competence, I give them several pieces whose sizes I already know, and they measure and record each one without help. If the results agree with mine within one division on every piece, and they clean and store the micrometer correctly, I sign them off on the training record.
markingPoints: Explains purpose, range and the names of the parts
Shows cleaning and the zero check
Demonstrates the method step by step, including the ratchet and reading the scales
Trainee practises under supervision with faults corrected
Checks competence with known pieces, compares results, and records the sign-off

essays.stem: Describe what a dimensional inspection report for a fabricated item should contain, and explain why each part of it matters.
essays.modelAnswer: The report starts with the job details: the job number, the item, the drawing number and its revision, and the customer, so that everyone knows exactly what was checked and against which drawing. It lists the devices used, each with its identification number and calibration due date, so the results can be trusted and traced. The main part is a table with each feature, the size and tolerance on the drawing, the measured size and whether it is accepted or rejected. Writing the actual size, not just 'OK', shows how close each one is to its limits and helps find trends. Any feature out of limit is marked clearly, with the action taken, such as a non-conformance report or a repair, so nothing faulty is passed by mistake. The report also notes the date, the temperature if it matters, and any comments, such as distortion seen. Finally, the inspector signs and dates it, and the supervisor reviews and signs it. It is then filed with the job records as proof of the checks.
markingPoints: Job details: job number, item, drawing number and revision
Devices used, with their numbers and calibration status
Table: feature, drawing size and tolerance, actual size, accept or reject
Out-of-limit features marked, with the action taken
Date, comments, signatures, review and filing, with reasons why each part matters

essays.stem: Draw up a care routine for your team's measuring devices in a welding shop in Jamaica's warm, humid and salty air. Say what is done at the end of each day, each week, and when a device needs repair.
essays.modelAnswer: At the end of each day, each user wipes their devices clean of dust, grinding grit and fingerprints with a clean cloth, puts a very light film of oil on bare steel parts, and returns them to their cases, with micrometer faces slightly apart and calipers unlocked. The cases go in a closed cabinet away from spatter, grinding and the welding bays. Digital devices are switched off and kept dry. Each week, the team leader checks every device: zeros, smooth movement, clear scales, tape hooks and blades, batteries, and calibration labels. Any rust is gently removed and the part re-oiled. Devices that have become magnetised from being near welding leads or magnetic bases are demagnetised, as the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules allow. A small pack of drying sachets in the cabinet helps keep the air dry. If a device is dropped, damaged, sticking, rusty on its faces or out of limit, it is tagged 'Do not use', recorded in the register and sent for repair or replacement, never repaired by the trainee.
markingPoints: Daily: clean, light oil on bare steel, into cases, micrometer faces apart, stored away from spatter
Digital devices kept dry and switched off; drying sachets or similar for humid air
Weekly: leader checks zeros, movement, scales, batteries and labels
Deals with rust and magnetism as the maker allows
Damaged or faulty devices tagged, recorded and sent for repair, not repaired by trainees

practical1.title: Plan and carry out a dimensional and weld inspection of a fabricated item, and write the inspection report
practical1.brief: The assessor gives the team a welded item made at the Centre (for example a frame, a bracket with bored holes, or a short pipe spool) and its drawing. As a team, plan the inspection: list every feature with its size and tolerance, choose a suitable device for each one and say why on the plan, and check that each device is clean, zeroed and in date. Then measure the item: overall sizes with a tape or rule, holes and thicknesses with calipers and micrometers, angles with a bevel protractor, squareness with a square and feeler gauges, and the welds with a fillet weld gauge and a bridge cam gauge. Each member measures at least four features with at least two different devices, and a second member repeats one of their readings as a check. Record every reading on an inspection sheet with the device number, mark each feature accepted or rejected, and write a short inspection report with a non-conformance report for any feature out of limit. The team leader for the day signs the report. Photograph each stage below and add the photos and sheets to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the report is finished and the devices are cleaned and stored.
materials: A welded item and its drawing, chosen by the assessor
Steel tape, steel rule, vernier or digital caliper, outside micrometers, inside micrometer or bore gauge
Bevel protractor, engineer's square and feeler gauges
Fillet weld gauge and bridge cam weld gauge
Inspection planning sheet, inspection record sheets and non-conformance report forms
Clean cloths and the devices' cases
photos: The inspection plan, showing each feature, its tolerance and the device chosen
Devices being cleaned and zeroed before use
Members measuring the item with three different devices (one photo each)
A weld being checked with the fillet or bridge cam gauge
The completed inspection sheet with device numbers and accept or reject marks
The signed inspection report and any non-conformance report
checklist: Chose a suitable device for each feature and could explain the choice
Cleaned, zeroed and checked the calibration label of each device before use
Used each device correctly (right pressure, square to the work, read without parallax)
Readings were accurate when repeated by another member or the assessor
Recorded readings with units and device numbers, and judged accept or reject correctly
Contributed to the inspection report and any non-conformance report
Cleaned and stored the devices correctly at the end
safety: Wear safety boots, and gloves when handling the item; watch for sharp edges and burrs
Lift or turn the item with a team lift or lifting aid as the assessor directs
Make sure the item is cool and not connected to any welding lead before measuring
Keep the inspection area clear of cables and offcuts
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules

practical2.title: Run a calibration check of the team's measuring devices and set up a calibration register
practical2.brief: The assessor provides a set of the Centre's measuring devices (at least two calipers, two micrometers, a dial indicator, a bevel protractor and three steel tapes), with gauge blocks or setting standards, a reference tape and a surface plate. As a team, plan the session and set up a clean, cool checking area. Each member checks at least two devices: inspect for damage, check the zero, then measure gauge blocks or standards at a minimum of three points across the range, and record the true size, the reading and the error. Check the tapes against the reference tape and look at the hooks and blades. Compare every error with the limit the assessor gives. Set up or update a calibration register with each device's number, range, resolution, results, pass or fail, and next due date. Fit a status label to each device and tag any that fail 'Do not use'. Clean, oil and store every device correctly. Finally, the team gives a 10-minute toolbox talk to the class on looking after measuring devices in a welding shop, and every member speaks. Photograph each stage below and add the photos and the register to the group's practical.
materials: A set of the Centre's measuring devices, chosen by the assessor
Gauge blocks or setting standards, a reference tape and a surface plate
Calibration check sheets and a register (paper or spreadsheet)
Status labels and 'Do not use' tags
Clean lint-free cloths, light instrument oil and the devices' cases
Flip chart or paper for the toolbox talk
photos: The plan, showing which devices each member will check
A member checking a micrometer or caliper on a gauge block or standard
The tapes laid against the reference tape
A completed check sheet showing readings and errors
The calibration register, with status labels fitted to the devices
A failed device tagged 'Do not use'
The devices cleaned and stored, and the team giving the toolbox talk
checklist: Inspected each device for damage and checked its zero correctly
Measured the standards at several points across the range with correct technique
Worked out and recorded each error correctly
Compared the errors with the limit and made the right pass or fail decision
Filled in the register and labels clearly and tagged failed devices
Handled gauge blocks carefully and cleaned, oiled and stored devices correctly
Spoke clearly in the toolbox talk on care of measuring devices
safety: Handle gauge blocks and standards with a clean cloth or gloves; do not drop them
Keep oils and cleaning products away from the eyes and wash hands after use
Work on a clean bench away from grinding, cutting and welding
Report any device that is damaged; do not try to repair it yourself
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
